gems.name: Garnet
gems.species: A team of related minerals (pyrope, almandine, spessartine, grossular, andradite, uvarovite and mixes)
gems.tagline: Not one gem but a whole team, in almost every color of the rainbow!
gems.what_it_is: Garnet is not just one mineral. It is a family of more than 20 related minerals. Five of them are the gem stars: pyrope, almandine, spessartine, grossular and andradite. Most gem garnets are a mix of two or more of them.
gems.colors: Red, purple-red, orange, yellow, brown, mint green, bright green, and even stones that change color. Not blue, except color-change garnets in daylight.
gems.where_found: Red garnet is found on every continent. Famous spots include India, Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Tanzania, Kenya, Namibia, Russia, the Czech Republic and the United States.
history: Thousands of years ago, red garnet necklaces were worn by Egypt's pharaohs.
In ancient Rome, people carved garnets into signet rings and used them to stamp the wax that sealed important letters.
Around the year 1500, big garnet deposits were found in Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), and "Bohemian garnet" jewelry became famous.
gems.cool_fact: Some garnets are rarer than others. Green tsavorite is much rarer than red garnet, because it needs very unusual rock chemistry to grow.
gems.care_tip: Garnets are pretty tough. Clean them with warm soapy water and try not to bang the corners on hard things.

varieties.name: Almandine
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The classic deep red garnet. Iron gives it its color.
varieties.where_found: India, Sri Lanka, Brazil, Madagascar, and Idaho and Alaska in the USA
varieties.fun_fact: Almandine crystals can grow right inside rocks, like raisins in a cake.

varieties.name: Pyrope
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The magnesium garnet. Old "Bohemian garnet" jewelry is pyrope.
varieties.where_found: Czech Republic (Bohemia), South Africa, Arizona and New Mexico, Tanzania, Sri Lanka
varieties.fun_fact: In Arizona and New Mexico, little pyrope garnets get carried to the surface by ants, so people call them "anthill garnets."

varieties.name: Rhodolite
varieties.color: Purplish red to raspberry and rose
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A purple-red mix of pyrope and almandine.
varieties.where_found: North Carolina (where it got its name), Tanzania, Kenya, Sri Lanka, India, Brazil
varieties.fun_fact: Its name comes from the Greek word "rhodon," which means rose. It was named in 1898.

varieties.name: Spessartine ("Mandarin" or "Fanta orange")
varieties.color: Bright orange, like an orange soda
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The manganese garnet. The brightest ones glow like a mandarin orange.
varieties.where_found: Namibia (Kunene River area), Nigeria, Tanzania, Mozambique, Madagascar, Brazil, USA
varieties.fun_fact: The famous "mandarin" orange garnets were first found in 1991 in the desert near the Kunene River in Namibia. Gem fans also call this color "Fanta orange."

varieties.name: Hessonite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: An orange kind of grossular garnet with a swirly inside.
varieties.fun_fact: Look inside with a magnifier and it can look wavy, like heat rising off a hot road. Its old nickname is "cinnamon stone."

varieties.name: Tsavorite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A green grossular garnet colored by vanadium and chromium. Rare and super sparkly.
varieties.where_found: Kenya and Tanzania (plus a little in Madagascar)
varieties.fun_fact: A geologist found it in Tanzania in 1967 and near Kenya's Tsavo National Park in 1970. It was named "tsavorite" after Tsavo in 1974. Most tsavorites are small, usually under 3 carats.

varieties.name: Merelani mint
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A paler, minty grossular. "Mint" is a nickname, not a lab name.
varieties.where_found: Merelani Hills, Tanzania (the same hills where tanzanite is found)
varieties.fun_fact: Labs just call it green grossular. "Mint garnet" is what gem lovers named it.

varieties.name: Demantoid
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A green andradite garnet with more rainbow "fire" than diamond.
varieties.where_found: Russia (Ural Mountains), Namibia, Madagascar, Italy, Pakistan
varieties.fun_fact: Its name means "diamond-like." Some Russian demantoids have curvy inclusions called "horsetails" that look like tiny horse tails inside the stone.

varieties.name: Topazolite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A yellow andradite garnet, cousin of demantoid.
varieties.fun_fact: It is named for looking like yellow topaz, but it is really a garnet.

varieties.name: Malaia (Malaya)
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A mix of pyrope and spessartine.
varieties.where_found: Umba Valley (Tanzania and Kenya), Madagascar, Sri Lanka, Mozambique
varieties.fun_fact: "Malaya" is a Swahili word meaning "out of the family," because miners first threw it away. Now people love it!

varieties.name: Color-change garnet
varieties.color: Blue-green in daylight, purple or red in lamp light
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The same stone looks like a different color when the light changes.
varieties.fun_fact: Take it from a sunny window to a cozy lamp and watch it switch colors like magic.

varieties.name: Mali garnet
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A mix of grossular and andradite.
varieties.fun_fact: It first showed up at gem shows in 1994, so it is one of the "newer" garnets.

varieties.name: Uvarovite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A chromium garnet whose crystals are usually too tiny to cut.
varieties.fun_fact: It grows as glittery green crusts of tiny crystals, like green sugar sprinkles on a rock.

gems.name: Ruby
gems.tagline: The king of red gems, and secretly a sapphire!
gems.what_it_is: Ruby is the red kind of the mineral corundum. Every other color of corundum is called sapphire. A little bit of chromium makes ruby red.
gems.colors: Red, from pinkish red to purplish red and orangy red. The very best is a pure, glowing red.
gems.where_found: Myanmar (the famous Mogok valley), Mozambique, Thailand and Cambodia, Vietnam, Madagascar, Tanzania, Afghanistan, Tajikistan and even Greenland.
history: The Carmen Lucia Ruby is a 23.10-carat ruby from Mogok, Myanmar. It was given to the Smithsonian museum in 2004.
The DeLong Star Ruby (100.32 carats) at the American Museum of Natural History was stolen in 1964 and then recovered!
The name "pigeon's blood" for the best red rubies goes back to an account written in 1888.
gems.cool_fact: Some rubies glow red even in sunlight! Rubies with very little iron light up under ultraviolet light, and the best ones seem to glow in daylight too.
gems.care_tip: Ruby is very hard, so it is great for everyday jewelry. Clean it with warm soapy water and a soft brush.

varieties.name: Burmese "pigeon's blood" ruby
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Rubies from marble rock with very little iron, so they glow red.
varieties.fun_fact: "Pigeon's blood" is a special name for the most glowing reds. A gem lab decides if a ruby earns it.

varieties.name: Mozambique ruby
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Bright, clear rubies with a little more iron, so they glow a bit less.
varieties.fun_fact: Mozambique now sends out huge numbers of beautiful rubies, which made it one of the world's big ruby spots.

varieties.name: Star ruby
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Tiny needle-shaped crystals inside bounce light into a moving star.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Myanmar and other ruby places
varieties.fun_fact: The Rosser Reeves Star Ruby (138.7 carats, Sri Lanka) lives at the Smithsonian. Very rarely a stone shows a 12-ray star!

varieties.name: Trapiche ruby
varieties.color: Red with a six-spoke wheel pattern
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Dark "spokes" of inclusions make a pattern that does not move.
varieties.fun_fact: "Trapiche" is a Spanish word for the wheel of a sugar-cane mill.

varieties.name: Greenland ruby
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Ruby from rock about 3 billion years old.
varieties.fun_fact: Yes, rubies come from icy Greenland too! Mining started there around 2017.

varieties.name: Ruby in zoisite (anyolite)
varieties.color: Pink-red ruby in green rock with black specks
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Not a single gem but a colorful rock: ruby crystals inside green zoisite.
varieties.fun_fact: It looks like a slice of watermelon candy, with green, pink and black all together.

varieties.name: Winza ruby
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Shiny ruby crystals found in Tanzania.
varieties.fun_fact: Winza had a ruby rush in 2007 and 2008.

gems.name: Sapphire
gems.tagline: Ruby's twin, in every color except red.
gems.what_it_is: Sapphire is corundum of any color except red (red corundum is ruby). Plain "sapphire" means blue. Other colors get a color name, like "yellow sapphire."
gems.colors: Blue most of all, plus pink, purple, orange, yellow, green, teal, white (colorless), black, and even stones that change color.
gems.where_found: Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Myanmar, Tanzania, Australia, Thailand and Cambodia, Montana in the USA, and the famous old mines of Kashmir.
history: Kashmir sapphires were found around 1881 after a landslide uncovered them high in the mountains.
In 1895 a gold miner in Montana found little "blue pebbles" in Yogo Gulch. They turned out to be sapphires!
The Star of India is a giant 563.35-carat star sapphire from Sri Lanka at the American Museum of Natural History.
gems.cool_fact: Blue sapphire gets its color from iron and titanium, and it only needs a tiny pinch: hundredths of a percent!
gems.care_tip: Sapphire is super hard (9 out of 10), so it is great for rings. Warm soapy water keeps it sparkling.

varieties.name: Blue sapphire
varieties.color: Blue, from light to deep, sometimes a little violet
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The classic sapphire. Iron and titanium make the blue.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Madagascar, East Africa, Australia, Thailand
varieties.fun_fact: The Logan Sapphire (422.99 carats, Sri Lanka) is one of the biggest blue sapphires at the Smithsonian. The Bismarck Sapphire necklace holds a 98.6-carat blue sapphire from Myanmar.

varieties.name: Kashmir "cornflower" sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Tiny inclusions make the blue look soft and velvety.
varieties.fun_fact: Hardly any have been mined since the 1880s, so they are some of the rarest sapphires.

varieties.name: Yogo sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: American sapphires that are naturally a great color.
varieties.fun_fact: Most Yogo sapphires are smaller than 1 carat, and they do not need heating to look great.

varieties.name: Padparadscha
varieties.color: Soft pinkish orange, like a sunset
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A rare pastel mix of pink and orange.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka is the classic source. Also Madagascar, Tanzania and Vietnam.
varieties.fun_fact: The name comes from an old Sri Lankan (Sinhalese) word linked to the lotus flower.

varieties.name: Pink sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Chromium makes it pink. Too dark red and it becomes a ruby!
varieties.where_found: Madagascar, Sri Lanka, East Africa, Myanmar
varieties.fun_fact: There is no single magic line between pink sapphire and ruby. Gem labs compare stones to decide.

varieties.name: Yellow sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Iron makes the yellow.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Tanzania, Australia, Thailand, Montana (USA) and Malawi
varieties.fun_fact: Some yellow sapphires glow red under a special UV light.

varieties.name: Orange sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Pink chromium plus a natural yellow color center add up to orange.
varieties.fun_fact: It is like color mixing in art class: pink + yellow = orange.

varieties.name: Purple sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Red chromium plus blue iron-titanium make purple.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Madagascar, Tanzania, Myanmar, Montana
varieties.fun_fact: About 3 out of every 100 Yogo sapphires from Montana are purple.

varieties.name: Green, teal and parti sapphire
varieties.color: Green, blue-green, or two colors in one stone
varieties.what_makes_it_special: "Parti" stones show zones of blue, green and yellow together.
varieties.where_found: Australia, Thailand, Montana and other basalt areas
varieties.fun_fact: "Teal" and "parti" are gem-lover nicknames, not lab names.

varieties.name: Color-change sapphire
varieties.color: Blue in daylight, purple in lamp light
varieties.what_makes_it_special: It switches color when the light changes.
varieties.fun_fact: The bigger the switch, the more special the stone.

varieties.name: White sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Very pure corundum with almost no coloring elements.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka and other sapphire places
varieties.fun_fact: It is colorless, but it is still the same super-hard mineral as ruby.

varieties.name: Star sapphire
varieties.color: Blue, violet, gray or black with a six-ray star
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Tiny needle crystals inside reflect light into a star that glides across the stone.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Myanmar and other sapphire places
varieties.fun_fact: The Star of Asia (about 330 carats, Myanmar) and the Star of Bombay (182 carats, Sri Lanka) are both at the Smithsonian.

varieties.name: Black star sapphire
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Hematite inside makes it black.
varieties.where_found: Thailand, Australia and other basalt areas
varieties.fun_fact: Its star can look silver or even gold.

gems.name: Emerald
gems.tagline: The green treasure that ancient peoples mined long ago.
gems.what_it_is: Emerald is the green kind of the mineral beryl. Chromium and vanadium make the green. If a green beryl is too light or gets its green from iron, it is called "green beryl" instead.
gems.colors: Bluish green to pure green. The best is rich and even.
gems.where_found: Colombia, Zambia, Brazil, Zimbabwe, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Russia and Ethiopia.
history: The Muisca people of Colombia mined emeralds long before the Spanish arrived.
Spanish explorers reached Colombia's emerald area in 1537 and found the mines that became famous as Chivor.
The Hooker Emerald (75.47 carats) was once owned by an Ottoman sultan. Today it is at the Smithsonian.
gems.cool_fact: Almost every emerald has tiny cracks inside. Gem cutters often fill them with oil so the stone looks clearer.
gems.care_tip: Never put an emerald in a steam cleaner or an ultrasonic cleaner. They can push out the oil in its cracks. Wipe it gently instead.

varieties.name: Colombian emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Colored by both chromium and vanadium. Often has tiny calcite and pyrite crystals inside.
varieties.fun_fact: Some Colombian emerald crystals glow red-pink under UV light, like in this photo from Muzo.

varieties.name: Zambian emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Usually darker and bluer than Colombian emerald.
varieties.fun_fact: Kagem is called the world's largest open-pit emerald mine.

varieties.name: Russian emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Old, famous emeralds from the Ural Mountains.
varieties.fun_fact: The story says a farmer found the first one around 1830.

varieties.name: Brazilian emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Brazil has several emerald areas.
varieties.fun_fact: This crystal is from Carnaiba in Bahia.

varieties.name: Pakistani (Swat) emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Small, bright crystals from mountain mines.
varieties.fun_fact: Swat has also produced trapiche emeralds.

varieties.name: Sandawana emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Tiny but very bright emeralds.
varieties.fun_fact: Cut Sandawana emeralds are usually tiny, often less than a quarter of a carat.

varieties.name: Trapiche emerald
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A fixed six-spoke wheel pattern from inclusions trapped while the crystal grew.
varieties.fun_fact: "Trapiche" is Spanish for a sugar-cane mill wheel, and that is just what it looks like.

gems.name: Aquamarine
gems.what_it_is: Aquamarine is the blue to greenish-blue kind of beryl, the same mineral as emerald. Iron gives it its color.
gems.colors: Light blue, sky blue, greenish blue and deep blue.
gems.where_found: Brazil (Minas Gerais), Nigeria, Madagascar, Mozambique, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Namibia and Russia.
history: The biggest aquamarine crystal on record was found in Brazil in 1910. It weighed 110 kilograms!
The Dom Pedro is a 10,363-carat aquamarine carved into a tall tower shape. It went on display at the Smithsonian in 2012.
gems.cool_fact: Turn an aquamarine and its color shifts: bluer one way, paler the other way. Most aquamarine is also gently heated to make it bluer.
gems.care_tip: Aquamarine is pretty hard, but it can chip if hit hard. Settings that hug the edges help protect it.

varieties.name: Santa Maria aquamarine
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A trade name for the deepest blues.
varieties.where_found: Named after the Santa Maria de Itabira mine in Brazil; also Mozambique
varieties.fun_fact: "Santa Maria" is a nickname that the gem world uses, not a lab name.

varieties.name: Maxixe beryl
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Its blue comes from natural radiation, not iron.
varieties.fun_fact: Leave it in sunlight and its blue slowly fades away!

varieties.name: Morganite (beryl cousin)
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Pink beryl colored by manganese.
varieties.where_found: Madagascar, Brazil, Afghanistan, Mozambique, Namibia and California (USA)
varieties.fun_fact: It was named in 1911 after the banker J.P. Morgan.

varieties.name: Heliodor or golden beryl (beryl cousin)
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Yellow beryl colored by iron.
varieties.fun_fact: "Heliodor" comes from "helios," the Greek word for sun.

varieties.name: Goshenite (beryl cousin)
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Beryl with almost no coloring elements.
varieties.fun_fact: It is named after Goshen, a town in Massachusetts.

varieties.name: Red beryl (beryl cousin)
varieties.what_makes_it_special: One of the rarest beryls. Manganese makes it red.
varieties.fun_fact: Utah is the only place in the world that has mined gem red beryl. Cut stones are usually smaller than 1 carat.

gems.name: Spinel
gems.tagline: The secret gem hiding in royal crowns.
gems.what_it_is: Spinel is its own mineral, made of magnesium, aluminum and oxygen. For hundreds of years, people mixed up red spinel with ruby.
gems.colors: Red, hot pink, neon pink, orange-pink, purple, lavender, gray, blue, cobalt blue and black.
gems.where_found: Myanmar (Mogok), Sri Lanka, Vietnam (Luc Yen), Tanzania (Mahenge), Tajikistan, and Pakistan.
history: The famous "Black Prince's Ruby" in England's Imperial State Crown is really a red spinel of about 170 carats.
Legend says King Henry V wore it at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415.
The Timur Ruby (352.5 carats) has old Persian names carved into it. People thought it was a ruby until 1851!
gems.cool_fact: Gem experts have called spinel "History's Most Underappreciated Gem," because it was so often mistaken for ruby and sapphire.
gems.care_tip: Spinel is hard (8 out of 10) and tough, so it makes great jewelry. Warm soapy water is all it needs.

varieties.name: Burmese red and "Jedi" spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Super-bright spinels with almost no dark areas and very little iron.
varieties.where_found: Mogok area (Man Sin and Namya), Myanmar
varieties.fun_fact: Gem experts nicknamed the brightest ones "Jedi" spinels, because they are "untouched by the dark side," like in Star Wars!

varieties.name: Mahenge spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Bright pink spinels from marble rocks.
varieties.fun_fact: In August 2007, miners found four giant spinel crystals there, weighing from 6 to 54 kilograms!

varieties.name: Cobalt blue spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A blue spinel colored mostly by cobalt. It is very rare.
varieties.fun_fact: To earn the cobalt name, a lab has to see that cobalt, not iron, makes the blue.

varieties.name: Vietnam pastel spinel
varieties.color: Baby pink to pastel purple, sometimes red
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Soft, sweet colors from rice-field gem gravels.
varieties.fun_fact: Serious spinel mining in Luc Yen started after 1990.

varieties.name: Lavender and purple spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Cool, calm colors. Some shift a little in warm light.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Vietnam and Tanzania
varieties.fun_fact: Check it under a warm lamp: some purples change color a tiny bit.

varieties.name: Kuh-i-Lal spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The historic source of many royal "balas rubies."
varieties.where_found: Kuh-i-Lal mines on the Panj River, Tajikistan
varieties.fun_fact: The mines are said to have been discovered after an earthquake in the 600s.

varieties.name: Black spinel
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Spinel with lots of iron.
varieties.where_found: Sri Lanka and other gem gravels
varieties.fun_fact: Sri Lankan gem gravels give spinels in pastel colors and in black too.

gems.name: Tourmaline
gems.species: Mostly elbaite (one of more than 14 tourmaline minerals)
gems.tagline: The rainbow gem: more colors than almost any other.
gems.what_it_is: Tourmaline is a family of more than 14 minerals. One of them, elbaite, makes almost all tourmaline gems. Different elements make different colors: iron for green and blue, manganese for pink and red, and copper for neon blue.
gems.colors: Every color: pink, red, green, blue, neon blue-green, yellow, brown, black, and stones with two or three colors at once.
gems.where_found: Brazil, Mozambique, Nigeria, Madagascar, Zambia, Tanzania, Afghanistan, Namibia, and Maine and California in the USA.
history: Electric-blue Paraiba tourmaline was first found in Brazil in August 1988, and reached gem markets in 1989.
One tourmaline mineral, liddicoatite, is named after a famous gemologist, Richard T. Liddicoat.
gems.cool_fact: One little pocket in a rock can hold tourmalines of many different colors, and a single crystal can be pink inside and green outside!
gems.care_tip: Tourmaline is fairly hard. Clean it with warm soapy water and keep it away from big heat.

varieties.name: Rubellite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Red and pink tourmaline colored by manganese.
varieties.where_found: Brazil, Nigeria, Mozambique, Madagascar, California and Maine (USA), Russia
varieties.fun_fact: Some gem fans only use the name rubellite for the redder ones, not the pinks.

varieties.name: Indicolite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Blue tourmaline colored by iron.
varieties.where_found: Brazil, Afghanistan, Namibia, Nigeria and Madagascar
varieties.fun_fact: It looks darker when you look down the long side of the crystal.

varieties.name: Verdelite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Green tourmaline colored by iron.
varieties.where_found: Brazil, Namibia, Afghanistan, Nigeria, Madagascar and Mozambique
varieties.fun_fact: Green tourmaline can look like two different greens from two sides.

varieties.name: Paraiba tourmaline
varieties.color: Neon blue, electric blue, blue-green to green
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Copper makes it glow like neon.
varieties.where_found: Brazil (Sao Jose da Batalha, Paraiba), Mozambique, Nigeria
varieties.fun_fact: It was first found in 1988 after years of digging in Paraiba, Brazil. Now any copper tourmaline with this glow can be called Paraiba.

varieties.name: Watermelon tourmaline
varieties.color: Pink center with a green rim
varieties.what_makes_it_special: One crystal grew pink first and then green.
varieties.where_found: Brazil, Madagascar, Maine and California (USA), Namibia, Mozambique
varieties.fun_fact: Cut it into slices and it looks just like a watermelon slice!

varieties.name: Bicolor (parti-color) tourmaline
varieties.color: Two or three colors in one stone
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Color zones that show when the crystal is cut the long way.
varieties.fun_fact: The color zones show how the crystal grew, like tree rings.

varieties.name: Chrome tourmaline
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Colored mostly by vanadium, even though it is called "chrome."
varieties.fun_fact: It is a different tourmaline mineral (dravite-uvite) from most other gem tourmalines.

varieties.name: Cat's-eye tourmaline
varieties.color: Any color with a bright line of light
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Tiny tubes inside make a shiny line, like a cat's eye.
varieties.fun_fact: Tilt it and the line slides across the stone.

varieties.name: Canary tourmaline
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Yellow elbaite rich in manganese.
varieties.fun_fact: It is named after the mining area, and its color fits a canary bird too.

varieties.name: Uvite and dravite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Magnesium tourmalines from marble rocks.
varieties.fun_fact: These tourmalines grow in old limestone that turned into marble.

gems.name: Quartz
gems.tagline: The super-common crystal with a giant family.
gems.what_it_is: Quartz is made of just silicon and oxygen. It has a huge family: amethyst, citrine, rose quartz, smoky quartz, tiger's eye, and even agate are all quartz!
gems.colors: Clear, purple, yellow, pink, brown-gray, green, and more.
gems.cool_fact: Our gem notes list about 19 different named kinds of quartz, plus another 14 kinds of chalcedony (quartz made of crystals too tiny to see).
gems.care_tip: Quartz is a 7 on the hardness scale, so it is pretty tough. Wash with warm soapy water.

varieties.name: Rock crystal
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Pure quartz with nothing coloring it.
varieties.fun_fact: Rock crystal can be carved into crystal balls!

varieties.name: Smoky quartz
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Quartz with a smoky look.
varieties.fun_fact: It is still quartz, just in a smoky outfit.

varieties.name: Ametrine
varieties.color: Purple and yellow in one stone
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Amethyst and citrine together in a single crystal.
varieties.fun_fact: Its name mixes the words "amethyst" and "citrine."

varieties.name: Prasiolite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Green quartz.
varieties.fun_fact: It is on our list of quartz varieties.

varieties.name: Star rose quartz
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Rose quartz that can show a star of light.
varieties.fun_fact: A star needs tiny needles inside the stone to bounce the light.

gems.name: Amethyst
gems.what_it_is: Amethyst is the purple kind of quartz. It is the same mineral as clear rock crystal and yellow citrine.
gems.colors: Light lilac to deep purple.
gems.cool_fact: Amethyst and citrine can grow together in the same crystal. That two-color stone is called ametrine!
gems.care_tip: Keep amethyst out of strong sunlight for long times, and clean it with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Citrine
gems.what_it_is: Citrine is the yellow to orange kind of quartz.
gems.colors: Lemon yellow to golden orange.
gems.cool_fact: Citrine is a cousin of amethyst. Sometimes they share a crystal, making ametrine.
gems.care_tip: Tough enough for everyday wear. Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Rose Quartz
gems.what_it_is: Rose quartz is the pink kind of quartz. It is usually cloudy instead of crystal-clear.
gems.colors: Pale to medium pink.
gems.cool_fact: Some rose quartz shows a star of light when it is cut into a dome shape.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Agate
gems.species: Chalcedony, a quartz made of tiny crystals
gems.what_it_is: Agate is a kind of chalcedony. Chalcedony is quartz made of crystals so tiny you cannot see them, even with a magnifier.
gems.colors: Every color, often in bands and stripes.
gems.cool_fact: Chalcedony has a big family too: agate, carnelian, chrysoprase, bloodstone, jasper and even petrified wood!
gems.care_tip: Agate is tough. Clean with warm soapy water.

varieties.name: Carnelian
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A see-through orange chalcedony.
varieties.fun_fact: It is on our chalcedony family list.

varieties.name: Chrysoprase
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A green chalcedony.
varieties.fun_fact: It is on our chalcedony family list.

varieties.name: Fire agate
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Agate with fiery rainbow colors inside.
varieties.fun_fact: The colors sparkle as you turn it.

varieties.name: Moss agate
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Agate with green patterns that look like moss or tiny plants.
varieties.fun_fact: The "moss" is really minerals, not plants!

gems.name: Tiger's Eye
gems.what_it_is: Tiger's eye is a kind of quartz. It is chatoyant, which means it shows a shiny band of light that moves, like a cat's eye.
gems.colors: Golden brown with shiny stripes.
gems.cool_fact: Turn it in the light and the shiny stripes roll across the stone.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Bloodstone
gems.what_it_is: Bloodstone is a kind of chalcedony, the tiny-crystal quartz family.
gems.colors: Dark green with red spots.
gems.cool_fact: It is part of the same chalcedony family as agate.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Opal
gems.tagline: The gem with rainbows trapped inside.
gems.what_it_is: Opal is silica (like quartz) with water inside, up to about 20 percent water! It has no crystal shape at all. Tiny stacked balls of silica bend light into flashes of color, called play-of-color.
gems.colors: White, black, clear, and orange-red fire opal, with rainbow flashes.
gems.where_found: Australia (about 90 percent of the world's opal), Ethiopia and Mexico.
history: The 998-gram "Fire of Australia" came from South Australia.
Lightning Ridge in Australia is famous for black opal.
gems.cool_fact: Australia produces about 90 percent of the world's opal. A huge opal called the "Fire of Australia" weighs 998 grams!
gems.care_tip: Opal is soft and has water inside. Keep it away from heat, harsh chemicals and big bumps.

varieties.name: Black opal
varieties.color: Dark body with bright rainbow flashes
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The dark background makes the colors pop.
varieties.fun_fact: Experts rate darkness from N1 (black) to N9 (white).

varieties.name: White (light) opal
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The classic milky opal with color flashes.
varieties.fun_fact: Light opals are N7 to N9 on the darkness scale.

varieties.name: Crystal opal
varieties.what_makes_it_special: You can see into the stone and the colors seem to float.
varieties.fun_fact: Experts love it when crystal opal is very clear.

varieties.name: Fire opal
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Bright warm body color, often without rainbow flashes.
varieties.fun_fact: It is also called "Mexican opal."

varieties.name: Boulder opal
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Opal veins in ironstone rock.
varieties.fun_fact: The rock is left on as a natural backing.

gems.name: Jade
gems.tagline: Two different rocks share one famous name.
gems.what_it_is: Jade is a name for two different tough rocks. Jadeite jade is made of tiny jadeite crystals. Nephrite jade is made of woven-together fibers. Both are super tough.
gems.colors: Green, white, lavender, and black. The bright green "imperial" jadeite is the most famous.
gems.where_found: Jadeite: Myanmar, Guatemala, Japan, Russia. Nephrite: China, Canada, New Zealand, Russia, Taiwan, USA.
history: Fei Cui is the historic Chinese name for jadeite jade.
China is the main place where jadeite is polished.
gems.cool_fact: Jadeite jade has an old Chinese name, Fei Cui.
gems.care_tip: Jade is very tough. Clean it with warm soapy water.

varieties.name: Jadeite jade
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Made of interlocked jadeite crystals.
varieties.fun_fact: Chromium gives the bright imperial green.

varieties.name: Nephrite jade
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Made of interlocked fibers, which makes it very tough.
varieties.where_found: China, Canada (British Columbia), New Zealand, Russia, Taiwan, USA
varieties.fun_fact: Its fibers lock together like felt.

gems.name: Turquoise
gems.tagline: The sky-blue stone of the desert.
gems.what_it_is: Turquoise is a mineral with copper in it. It forms in dry desert places, when water with copper soaks through the rocks.
gems.colors: Sky blue to blue-green, sometimes with brown or black lines.
gems.where_found: Only a few dry places: Iran, the USA (Arizona, Nevada, New Mexico), China, Egypt (Sinai) and Mexico.
history: Nishapur in Iran is a famous old turquoise source.
gems.cool_fact: The thin dark lines in some turquoise are bits of the rock it grew in. A fine web pattern is called "spiderweb" turquoise.
gems.care_tip: Turquoise is soft and porous. Keep it away from oils, lotions and chemicals.

gems.name: Tanzanite
gems.tagline: A gem from just one place on Earth.
gems.what_it_is: Tanzanite is the blue to purple kind of a mineral called zoisite. Vanadium gives it color.
gems.colors: Blue-violet, violet-blue and purple.
gems.where_found: Only the Merelani Hills in northern Tanzania, near Mount Kilimanjaro.
history: Tanzanite was discovered in 1967.
It was named after its home country, Tanzania.
gems.cool_fact: Tanzanite shows different colors from three directions. Turn it and it shifts between blue, violet and purple!
gems.care_tip: It is a bit softer than many gems. Wear it carefully and clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Alexandrite
gems.tagline: Green by day, red by lamplight!
gems.what_it_is: Alexandrite is a rare kind of chrysoberyl with chromium inside. It changes color depending on the light.
gems.colors: Green to bluish green in daylight; red to purplish red in lamp light.
gems.where_found: Russia (Ural Mountains, the classic source), Sri Lanka, Brazil, East Africa and India.
history: The first famous alexandrites came from the Ural Mountains in Russia.
Brazilian alexandrite can be as fine as Russian.
gems.cool_fact: Only chrysoberyl gets to be called alexandrite. Other gems that change color are called "color-change" gems instead.
gems.care_tip: Alexandrite is very hard. Clean it with warm soapy water.

varieties.name: Cat's-eye chrysoberyl (cymophane)
varieties.color: Honey yellow with a line of light
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A chrysoberyl that shows a cat's-eye line.
varieties.fun_fact: It is listed on our chrysoberyl species card.

gems.name: Pearl
gems.tagline: A gem made by a living animal.
gems.what_it_is: A pearl grows inside a mollusk, like an oyster or mussel. Natural pearls form around a tiny bit of something, with no help from people. Cultured pearls are started by people.
gems.colors: White, cream, silver, gold, gray, black and brown, with shimmery overtones.
gems.where_found: Oceans, lakes and rivers. Akoya: Japan and China. South Sea: Australia, Indonesia, Philippines, Myanmar. Tahitian: French Polynesia.
gems.cool_fact: Tahitian pearls from French Polynesia can be gray, black or brown.
gems.care_tip: Pearls are very soft. Put them on last, after lotion and hairspray, and wipe them with a soft cloth.

varieties.name: Akoya pearl
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Saltwater pearl.
varieties.fun_fact: Akoya pearls grow in the sea.

varieties.name: South Sea pearl
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Grown in a big oyster.
varieties.fun_fact: They come from a large oyster called Pinctada maxima.

varieties.name: Tahitian pearl
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Dark pearls with colorful glows.
varieties.fun_fact: Look for green, pink or purple glows on top.

varieties.name: Freshwater pearl
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Grown in lakes and rivers.
varieties.fun_fact: They grow in fresh water, not the sea.

gems.name: Diamond
gems.tagline: The hardest natural gem: a perfect 10.
gems.what_it_is: Diamond is made of pure carbon, like pencil lead, but packed into a super-strong crystal.
gems.colors: Colorless, plus rare "fancy" colors like yellow, pink, blue and green.
gems.where_found: Russia, Angola, Botswana, Canada, DR Congo, Namibia and South Africa.
history: Golconda in India is a famous historic diamond area.
GIA created the 4Cs: color, clarity, cut and carat.
gems.cool_fact: Some blue diamonds can carry electricity!
gems.care_tip: Diamond is the hardest, but it can still chip if hit hard. Clean with warm soapy water.

varieties.name: Pink diamond
varieties.what_makes_it_special: A rare natural pink.
varieties.fun_fact: The Argyle mine was famous for pinks.

varieties.name: Blue diamond
varieties.what_makes_it_special: Contains a little boron, so it can carry electricity.
varieties.fun_fact: It conducts electricity!

gems.name: Topaz
gems.what_it_is: Topaz is its own mineral, with aluminum, silicon and fluorine. Golden "imperial" topaz is a famous kind.
gems.colors: Colorless, blue, golden orange, pink.
gems.cool_fact: Most bright blue topaz in jewelry got its color from a treatment.
gems.care_tip: Topaz can split along a flat line (called cleavage). Avoid bumps and ultrasonic cleaners.

varieties.name: Imperial topaz
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The famous golden kind.
varieties.fun_fact: It is on our topaz species list.

gems.name: Peridot
gems.what_it_is: Peridot is the gem kind of a mineral called olivine, made of magnesium, iron, silicon and oxygen.
gems.colors: Yellow-green to olive green.
gems.cool_fact: Iron gives peridot its green.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Moonstone
gems.what_it_is: Moonstone is a kind of feldspar, one of the most common minerals on Earth.
gems.colors: White to clear with a blue or white glow.
gems.cool_fact: Moonstone is a cousin of sunstone, labradorite and amazonite. They are all feldspars!
gems.care_tip: Moonstone is fairly soft. Avoid bumps.

gems.name: Sunstone
gems.what_it_is: Sunstone is a feldspar with sparkly flakes inside.
gems.colors: Orange, red, peach, with glittery sparkles.
gems.cool_fact: Sunstone and moonstone are both feldspars.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Labradorite
gems.what_it_is: Labradorite is a feldspar that flashes blue, green and gold.
gems.colors: Gray with flashes of blue, green, gold.
gems.cool_fact: Spectrolite is a kind of labradorite that shows the rainbow colors especially well.
gems.care_tip: Avoid bumps.

gems.name: Amazonite
gems.what_it_is: Amazonite is the green-blue kind of microcline, a feldspar.
gems.colors: Mint green to blue-green.
gems.cool_fact: It is a feldspar, like moonstone.
gems.care_tip: Avoid bumps.

gems.name: Zircon
gems.what_it_is: Zircon is a natural mineral made of zirconium, silicon and oxygen.
gems.colors: Blue, brown, red, yellow, colorless.
gems.cool_fact: Natural zircon is not the same as cubic zirconia, which is made in a lab.
gems.care_tip: Edges can chip. Store it apart from other gems.

gems.name: Kunzite
gems.tagline: Pink power from a lithium mineral.
gems.what_it_is: Kunzite is the pink kind of spodumene, a mineral with lithium in it.
gems.colors: Pink to lilac.
gems.cool_fact: Its green cousin is called hiddenite. Both are spodumene.
gems.care_tip: Keep kunzite out of strong sunlight, which can fade it.

varieties.name: Hiddenite
varieties.what_makes_it_special: The green kind of spodumene.
varieties.fun_fact: It is kunzite's green cousin.

gems.name: Iolite
gems.what_it_is: Iolite is the gem name for cordierite.
gems.colors: Violet-blue.
gems.cool_fact: It looks different colors from different sides.
gems.care_tip: Clean with warm soapy water.

gems.name: Lapis Lazuli
gems.species: Lapis lazuli, a rock made mostly of lazurite
gems.what_it_is: Lapis lazuli is a rock, not a single mineral. Its blue comes mostly from lazurite.
gems.colors: Deep royal blue, often with gold flecks.
gems.cool_fact: Because it is a rock, it is made of several minerals mixed together.
gems.care_tip: It is soft. Avoid chemicals and bumps.

gems.name: Malachite
gems.what_it_is: Malachite is a copper mineral with green bands and swirls.
gems.colors: Light and dark green bands.
gems.cool_fact: Copper gives malachite its green.
gems.care_tip: It is soft. Keep away from acids and bumps.

gems.name: Amber
gems.tagline: Ancient tree sap turned to gem.
gems.what_it_is: Amber is fossilized resin from ancient trees. It is organic, not a mineral.
gems.colors: Honey yellow, orange, brown.
gems.cool_fact: Amber is so light, some can float in salty water.
gems.care_tip: Very soft. Keep away from heat and chemicals.
